resource.name: Ghana G-SAM Impact Evaluation Endline Administrator Survey
resource.description: USAID’s Center of Excellence for Democracy, Human Rights and Governance contracted Social Impact, Inc. to conduct an impact evaluation of USAID’s Ghana Strengthening Accountability Mechanisms (G-SAM) program, which aimed to increase accountability of local District Assemblies in Ghana. This impact evaluation, a randomized-controlled trial, tested the effect of two distinct efforts to increase accountability and improve service delivery outcomes at the district level. One hundred fifty of Ghana’s districts were matched and randomized into one of three groups: a top-down treatment group that received performance audits conducted by the central government Ghana Audit Service (GAS); a bottom-up treatment group that received civil-society organization (CSO) led scorecard campaigns; and a control group that did not receive either intervention. Outcomes were measured across three surveys administered at baseline (2014) and endline (2017). This dataset specifically contains endline data from a survey targeted at district administrations, who are responsible for overseeing the contracting and construction of development projects.

domain_metadata.value: Julia Kresky, Ben Morse, Erik Wibbels. 2023. Ghana G-SAM Impact Evaluation Endline Administrator Survey. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/hm6e-u9cj.

As part of the de-identification process, we removed/recoded some geographic variables that may limit usability. In the household datasets, we removed village names and masked enumeration areas to prevent the risk of re-identification; this will prevent users from summarizing data at the village / EA levels, or tracking trends at these levels. Also to prevent the risk of re-identification, in the politician and administrator datasets, we removed district names and masked region names, which will make it impossible to associate responses with specific districts and regions.  Another limitation is that although the household survey was a panel survey, with the same households surveyed at baseline and endline, the household unique identifier is not available. As a result, households cannot be match across rounds and the data must be treated as a repeated cross section, rather than a panel survey.
Julia Kresky, Ben Morse, Erik Wibbels
Bureau for Development, Democracy, and Innovation

All datasets within this data asset have undergone an extensive de-identification process. The project team has reviewed each of the datasets individually for direct and indirect identifiers, including geographic variables. In consultation with Social Impact’s Institutional Review Board (IRB), we have removed all direct identifiers such as names, phone numbers, and physical addresses, as well as low-level geographic variables such as GPS coordinates, enumeration areas, and village names. We have also removed district names and encoded the region variable for the politician and administrator datasets due to the small number of politicians and administrators in each district and region. In addition, we recoded the age variable (transforming it from continuous to categorical) and recoded minority religious groups identified through the religion variable and minority tribal groups identified through the tribe variable as “Other.” We also reviewed all open-ended text variables and recoded any variables containing responses with potential PII as “missing.” This de-identified data asset has been approved for publication by the Social Impact IRB. Please see the USAID Data Services DDL Variable Manipulation Overview, 
https://data.usaid.gov/api/views/xw2i-z7hr/files/de8f1fd7-1803-43bf-9a5a-de5f67a57ccb, noting the risk mitigation techniques implemented in some data assets on the DDL, as well as examples of the impact of these techniques on the data.

The data included in this data asset was collected as part of an impact evaluation of the Ghana Strengthening Accountability Mechanism’s (G-SAM) project, which aimed to improve accountability at the district level in Ghana. We believe this data would be a valuable resource for other researchers studying government accountability and could even be used to inform future good governance interventions across West Africa. The politician and administrator datasets capture information on the education and position of district-level administrators and politicians in Ghana, the perceived importance/ranking of factors that determine political success, factors that influence the types/locations of development projects, the process of identifying contractors for development projects and common issues in the construction or of these projects, perceived government corruption at the district level, the performance and provision of government services, and government accountability. The household datasets contain information on citizens’ views on the quality of services in their district, perceived factors that influence the type and location of development projects, perceived reasons for issues or other delays with projects in their district, the quality of governance and the political environment in their district, their participation in district politics and level of political sophistication, reported factors that influence their vote, perceived government accountability in their district, and levels of social cohesion in their community. Since this data asset contains three baseline datasets and three endline datasets each containing a wide range of variables, researchers who use this data asset will be able to understand changes in the above factors in Ghana over the 3-year period between 2014 and 2017.

resource.description:
Feed the Future seeks to reduce poverty and undernutrition in 19 developing countries including Kenya by focusing on accelerating growth of the agricultural sector, addressing root causes of undernutrition, and reducing gender inequality.

This dataset (n=1,772, vars=18) contains data from sub-Module F2: Income Sources During Periods of Stress. Each household with data has a single record = 1,772 Module F households with sub-Module F2 data.

domain_metadata.value: Westat. 2023. Feed the Future Northern Kenya Zone of Influence Survey Baseline - Income Sources During Stress Dataset. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/hudi-67us.

All survey specific data elements should be removed as they are only useful in managing the implementation of the survey: date of interview, ability to be interviewed alone, outcome of the interview.

A range of household level data elements were reported in all other datasets and should be removed from all datasets except household’s. Examples include dwelling characteristics (roof, floor, walls) and hunger scale questions.

We will use the following steps to anonymize the datasets:
1.	Use k-anonymity to mitigate the following variables: sex, dwelling characteristics, relationship to household head, type of toilets, education level, literacy level (read and write), district, urbanization. To achieve a threshold of k=3, we will recode some of these variables including dwelling characteristics, type of toilets, relationship to household head, education level, and literacy level  
2.	Aggregate age variable into 5 ages bands. 
3.	Apply a micro aggregation to children and women weights and heights. Micro Aggregation replaces each single value with local means calculated on batches of 3 records each. 
4.	Top code the age and estimated price of house. Any reported house age value above 100 years was recoded as 100; any estimated price at 5 000 000 or above was replaced with the mean price of houses costing 5 000 000 or more. 
5.	      5. Capping household size to 13. To achieve this, we will randomly select out of the datasets individual members from these large households who do not participate anywhere else in the survey other than their membership to household. Initially, the largest household had 21 members; after this process, this household would have 13 members. The median household in Kenya is about 4.4. In this data, the median remains at 5.0 before and after households disclosure risk mitigation.

resource.name: Feed the Future Tanzania Mboga na Matunda Producer Survey 2018 - Module F Buyer Information
resource.description:
This dataset contains information on the buyers to whom producer beneficiaries sold horticultural produce, as recorded in the FY 18 producer survey.
This dataset is Module F of a data asset that contains data from the beneficiary based fiscal year 2018 annual results survey of smallholder producers assisted by the Feed the Future Tanzania - Mboga na Matunda Project. The project works to improve the livelihoods of horticultural farmers in the regions of Iringa, Morogoro, Songwe, Mbeya, and Zanzibar, and strengthen the market system throughout the ZOI. The survey sample was developed using a two-staged cluster design. In the first stage, 77 villages were selected for inclusion in the survey using the method of probability proportional to size based on beneficiary population data as recorded in FTFT-MnM's client database. In the second stage, 12 respondents were selected from each village. In total, 932 respondents were surveyed. The data is split into modules. Module A captures basic demographic data and landholdings. Module B captures information on the household members. Module C captures information on the dietary diversity of female household members. Modules D, E, F, G capture data on production of horticultural produce and associated costs, as well as information on sales. Module H captures information on access to finance.

resource.name: Farm Plots Survey for Agriculture for Children's Empowerment (ACE) in Liberia- Farm Plots Endline Dataset
resource.description: The STRIVE project, funded by USAID's Displaced Children and Orphans Fund (DCOF) and managed by FHI 360, used market-led economic strengthening initiatives to improve the well-being of vulnerable children. Through STRIVE, ACDI/VOCA implemented the Agriculture for Children’s Empowerment (ACE) Project in Liberia, which is founded on the premise that increased household economic security will stimulate more consistent investments in children’s well being via longer term social investments in education and nutrition. ACE’s primary focus was on the horticulture value chain (VC) — the production and marketing of vegetables by smallholder farmers in Montserrado, Bong, and Nimba counties of Liberia. ACE also strengthened smallholder rice farming to increase household food security using a market-sensitive approach to rice seed lending and cultivation.  This dataset contains endline information about each plot the household owns.

resource.name: Rift Valley Fever Innovation Lab: MP-12-NSm-del vaccine in livestock administered intradermally
resource.description:
In this study, livestock were vaccinated intradermally with 5 log10 pfu of MP-121-NSm-del Rift Valley fever live, attenuated vaccine using the Bioject Zetajet developmental device.  Neutralizing antibody titers (expressed as a reciprocal) were determined by the 80% Plaque Reduction Neutralization technique (PRNT-80) at days post vaccination (DPV). 

The overall purpose of the Feed the Future Innovation Lab for Rift Valley Fever Control in Agriculture is to increase the food supply by developing and applying a vaccine for the prevention of Rift Valley fever disease among livestock in Africa.  Rift Valley Fever (RVF) is a mosquito-borne viral disease that continues to have a devastating impact on human and animal health in Africa.  Since the discovery of RVF as the cause of an outbreak among sheep and humans during the early 1930s in the Rift Valley in Kenya, the disease has emerged as one of the most important zoonoses in Africa. The disease has and continues to affect the health of thousands to millions of humans and animals, and the livestock industry has lost millions of dollars, and therefore, affecting hundreds of millions of those whose livelihood depends on livestock, exaggerating poverty on already deprived communities.

The specific aim of the Lab is to conduct a 5 year research project to develop and evaluate a vaccine for the prevention of Rift Valley fever (RVF) among livestock in Tanzania and other RVF virus enzootic African regions and thereby improve food security, nutrition and livelihoods in Africa as a USAID priority under Feed the Future, the U.S. Government’s global hunger and food security initiative.  This data asset reports the results of this work.

resource.name: Genes Controlling Black Seed Coat and Pod Tip Color in Cowpea: List of genes in the overlapping significant region with annotations
resource.description: Seed coat color is an important part of consumer preferences for cowpea (Vigna unguiculata [L.] Walp). Color has been studied in numerous crop species and has often been linked to loci controlling the anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway. This study makes use of available resources, including mapping populations, a reference genome, and a high-density single nucleotide polymorphism genotyping platform, to map the black seed coat and purple pod tip color traits, with the gene symbol Bl, in cowpea. Several gene models encoding MYB domain protein 113 were identified as candidate genes. MYB domain proteins have been shown in other species to control expression of genes encoding enzymes for the final steps in the anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway. PCR analysis indicated that a presence/absence variation of one or more MYB113 genes may control the presence or absence of black pigment. A PCR marker has been developed for the MYB113 gene Vigun05g039500, a candidate gene for black seed coat color in cowpea.

domain_metadata.value: University of California Riverside. 2023. Genes Controlling Black Seed Coat and Pod Tip Color in Cowpea: List of genes in the overlapping significant region with annotations. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/hzxn-n45n.
Bureau for Resilience and Food Security

Advances in genomics over the past several years have enabled the elucidation the genetic basis of black seed coat and purple pod tip color, traits first described nearly one hundred years ago. This study maps black seed coat and purple pod tip color in several independently generated populations and provides candidate genes. Using high-throughput SNP genotyping and whole genome sequencing, previously impossible levels of mapping precision have been achieved. The presence of a deletion is supported by PCR evidence and sequence alignment from thirty-seven accessions. The identification of MYB transcription factors as candidate genes is supported by prior literature on homologous genes performing similar functions in other species, including Arabidopsis, grape, citrus, and soybean. The PCR-based markers developed here provide a useful tool for breeders engaged in marker-assisted selection for seed coat color in cowpea.

resource.name: PPL Evaluation Registry Dataset
resource.description: The Evaluation Registry is the main source for USAID evaluation reporting, including the number of evaluations completed by USAID operating units each year, and how evaluations are used. resource.description: This dataset captures early season aphid counts.  It contains 1,080 rows and 6 columns. Two experiments were conducted, one planted on 8/22/2018 (fall 2018) and another planted on 1/19/2019 (spring 2019), in Jonc-Labeille, Haiti. Three experimental treatments were compared: sorghum, sorghum intercropped with maize, and sorghum intercropped with pigeon pea. The sorghum variety was “Bout gode,” the maize variety was “Chicken corn,” and the pigeon pea was “Pwa kongo local.” A randomized complete block design experiment was used.

resource.name: Program Evaluation of USAID/Uganda SUSTAIN Activity: Ministry of Health Staff Data
resource.description:
USAID/Uganda’s Strengthening Uganda’s Systems for Treating AIDS Nationally (SUSTAIN) activity supports Uganda’s Ministry of Health (MOH) to strengthen quality and comprehensive HIV/AIDS care, prevention, laboratory and tuberculosis (TB) services at selected regional referral and district health care facilities in Uganda, as well as build the capacity of the public health system to sustain these services. SUSTAIN is a six­-year USAID­-funded activity launched in 2010 and implemented by University Research Co., LLC (URC). SUSTAIN is one of many PEPFAR-­funded activities to address the HIV/AIDS epidemic in Uganda. The main objective of the SUSTAIN program evaluation was to examine the activity’s methodology for achieving its
objectives in order to inform future USAID design work. USAID noted that URC had performed well on SUSTAIN, as evidenced by its activity reports, but wanted an evaluation of the approach used by SUSTAIN to inform future program designs. SUSTAIN implementation adapted to contextual changes in the Government of Uganda's (GoU) HIV/AIDS strategy responding to a spike in new infections and people living with HIV, and major shifts in PEPFAR policy.

domain_metadata.value: President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR)
Panagora Group. 2020. Program Evaluation of USAID/Uganda SUSTAIN Activity: Ministry of Health Staff Data. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/id5e-8vkj.
Although the evaluators did identify participants in the focus groups and key informant interviews, the data that could identify respondents was not included in any of the spreadsheets.

The dataset consists of recorded responses to a series of questions asked during key informant interviews (KII) or client focus groups regarding the delivery of HIV/AIDS related services. There are 11 spreadsheets, each recording the answers of a different set of actors in health service delivery: district health officers, focus groups comprised of clients (two spreadsheets), clinic staff, laboratory staff, implementing partners, lower level facility staff, Ministry of Health staff, regional referral hospital staff, SUSTAIN project staff, and USAID staff.

resource.name: Liberia Teacher Training Program II 2013 EGRA Midline
resource.description:
The Liberia Teacher Training Program II (LTTP II) is a partnership between FHI 360 and RTI International to provide support to the central Ministry of Education (MOE). The overarching goal of LTTP II is to enhance pupils' learning in general, and reading proficiency in particular; establish a functional teacher professional development (PD) system; and strengthen the MOE's capacity to manage such a system. The LTTP II was originally designed to work in nine counties: Grand Gedeh, Grand Kru, Lofa, Maryland, Montserrado, Nimba, River Cess, River Gee, and Sinoe. In 2011 and 2012, because of changes in USAID policies, the number of counties was reduced to five (i.e., Bong, Lofa, Margibi, Montserrado, and Nimba), which USAID identifies as a development corridor containing a majority of the Liberian population.

The LTTP II intervention drew on the EGRA Plus model to introduce similarly structured reading and math programs in grades 1, 2, and 3 to approximately 1,020 schools in four counties (i.e., Bong, Lofa, Montserrado, and Nimba) in a phased approach. Cohort 1, the first to receive support, had 792 schools. During the middle of the 2011/2012 school year, the reading program was introduced in all three grades in these schools. During the middle of the 2012/2013 school year, the mathematics program was introduced in all three grades. Cohort 2, consisting of approximately 330 schools, began participating in the programs reading and mathematics interventions during the 2013/2014 school year and continued during the 2014/2015 school year. Some changes, although not significant, were made to the intervention approach for supporting the Cohort 2 schools.

Schools in the four LTTP II counties were randomly assigned to the Cohort 1 and Cohort 2 groupings. These schools were then grouped in clusters of 12 schools based on geographic proximity, which would allow the program to deliver the interventions more efficiently

Cohort 1: Schools from the four target counties included in Cohort 1 served as the treatment group for the midterm assessment. These schools stopped receiving LTTP II support after the midterm assessment, but they participated in the endline assessment, as a way to determine whether the gains that were achieved during the treatment were sustained.

Cohort 2: Schools included in Cohort 2 in the same four counties began to receive treatment after the midterm assessment, thus, during the final two years of the program. Cohort 2 schools served as a control to which the Cohort 1 results were compared. The performance of Cohort 2 schools were to be compared to that of Cohort 1. The biggest challenge that the program faced regarding the implementation in Cohort 2 schools was the school closings because of the Ebola crisis. Schools were closed between September 2014 and February 2015. Even after the official reopening date, with the gradual actual opening of schools that required LTTP II to wait until schools were safe to open, it took several months to distribute books to schools and to train teachers which in turn severely affected the implementation of the treatment.

External Cohort: A randomly selected sample of schools outside the four target counties served as another comparator, especially after Cohort 2 began receiving treatment alongside Cohort 1.

Except for a small number of schools associated with the RTTIs, schools outside the four target counties did not participate in the program during the lifetime of LTTP II.

This data file contains the 2013 EGRA midline.

resource.name: Feed the Future South Sudan: Farmer-Based Organization Survey Data
resource.description: In order to better understand how the FARM II project reached farmer-based organizations (FBOs) and farmers across the Greenbelt region and how the project may have influenced beneficiaries to use improved technologies or management practices, FARM II conducted two process evaluations in March 2016. The evaluations were conducted in 28 payams across eight counties of Central, Eastern, and Western Equatoria states. This first evaluation, the FBO survey, assessed the technical and managerial capacity of elected leaders of farmer-based organizations that received assistance from the FARM II project. The second evaluation, the farmer survey, measured knowledge, attitudes, and the application of improved technologies and management practices by targeted farmer beneficiaries.

FARM II provides technical assistance and other services to improve agricultural markets and food security in the Greenbelt region of South Sudan. The project aims to increase agricultural productivity and improve the capacity of producers to develop commercial agriculture. resource.name: Feed The Future Interim Population-Based Assessment of Cambodia, Module D, Dwelling Characteristics
resource.description: This dataset captures characteristics of the dwellings sampled during the first interim assessment of Feed the Future’s population-based indicators for the ZOI in Cambodia.  The ZOI is the Pursat, Battambang, Kampong Thom, and Siem Reap Provinces.  The sampling design called for a two-stage cluster sample.  In the first stage, 84 villages were selected; in the second stage, households were selected within each sampled village. The sampling of villages was stratified by province, with the number of villages in each stratum proportional to the population in the stratum and with villages selected with probability proportional to size, based on the 2013 Commune Database.  The data is split into survey modules.  Modules A through C includes location information, informed consent, and the household roster.  Module D includes household characteristics.  Module E is the expenditures module broken up into 8 different parts.  Modules F and G include the hunger scale data and WEIA index data.  Data in modules H and I include mother and child dietary diversity.

resource.name: Breakthrough ACTION Malaria Behavior Survey - Malawi Household Dataset
resource.description: This Malaria Behavior Survey (MBS) dataset includes representative data on the determinants of malaria-related behaviors from urban and rural areas in the Northern, Central, and Southern regions of Malawi, collected between May 26th and July 1st 2021. The goal of this study was two-fold: 1) to provide a better understanding of the socio-demographic, attitudinal, and normative characteristics (also referred to as ideational characteristics) associated with malaria-related behavioral outcomes in the Northern, Central, and Southern regions of Malawi and 2) to determine the appropriate focus of programmatic activities designed to improve malaria-related ideational and behavioral outcomes. This study used a cross-sectional survey design with a random sample of women and men using structured questionnaires. Respondents were selected through a multi-step cluster random sampling approach. The research team collected relevant information from 3,862 households, which included 4,181 women of reproductive age and 1,304 of their male spouses/partners.

resource.name: MEASURE-BiH: High Judicial and Prosecutorial Council Administrative Data Dataset
resource.description:
Administrative data from the High Judicial and Prosecutorial Council (HJPC) of Bosnia and Herzegovina is one of the three datasets used to calculate the Judicial Effectiveness Index of Bosnia and Herzegovina (JEI-BiH), a groundbreaking tool for monitoring and evaluating judicial performance. Both BiH authorities and the international community have continuously supported justice sector reform in BiH for many years.

However, there is little evidence on the effectiveness of those interventions. Unlike any other rule of law or justice index, JEI-BiH combines three data sources to create an objective snapshot of the BiH judiciary. Administrative data on the caseload of BiH courts and prosecutors’ offices are paired with data on public perception and professional opinion collected through surveys of citizens’ perceptions and of judges and prosecutors in BiH.

The JEI-BiH was developed by USAID/MEASURE-BiH in close partnership with the BiH High Judicial and Prosecutorial Council. As such, it is not only a tool for donors but also for BiH authorities for informed decision-making and monitoring of progress towards establishing a more accountable, effective, and independent judiciary.

domain_metadata.value: IMPAQ International. 2019. MEASURE-BiH: High Judicial and Prosecutorial Council Administrative Data Dataset. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/jbf9-2yi7.

This data set provides combines data from three unique sources (administrative data, public perception data, and perception of judges/prosecutors in BiH) in the period 2015-2018. MEASURE-BIH used this data set to calculate the JEI-BIH, but the data available could be used by other researches on questions of interest, in particular those related to the BiH judiciary. Furthermore, any sub-set of data points can be isolated and used in other cross-sectional analysis related to a number of issues within the BiH justice system. While surveys of judges and prosecutors are common around the world, the JEI data set is unique in its systematic data collection process in the BiH judiciary, a rarity in the BIH context.

resource.name: Cross-sectional Survey of Urinary Aflatoxins and Diet Recall in Haiti
resource.description: Aflatoxins (AFs) are hepatocarcinogenic mycotoxins that can contaminate grains and oil seeds in tropical and sub-tropical areas and have been detected in maize and peanut products of Haiti. The first objective of our study was to assess human exposure to Afs among Haitians at an urban hospital (GHESKIO) and a rural health centre (HCBH). The second objective was to test the association between AF exposure and reported dietary intake of potentially contaminated foods, such as maize, peanut products and milk. Subjects were recruited at the Groupe Haitien d’Etude du Sarcome de Kaposi et des Infections Opportunistes Health Centre in Port-au-Prince (GHESKIO, n = 147) from 9–24 July 2012, and at the Hôpital Convention Baptiste d’Haïti in Quartier Morin (HCBH, n = 191) from 9 September 2013 to 7 February 2014. At HCBH, study subjects also included minors (1–17.9 years of age, n = 28). Intake of dairy, other animal-sourced foods, peanut products and maize was assessed using a dietary recall survey. Aflatoxin exposure was assessed by measurement of urinary Aflatoxin M1 using high pressure liquid chromatography.

resource.name: Malawi Baseline Impact Evaluation: Farmer Data
resource.description:
Feed the Future initiative in Malawi is committed to improving food security and nutrition in farming households while reducing rural poverty through an agriculture-­led, integrated economic growth, nutrition, and natural resource management strategy. The goal of the impact evaluation is to determine whether integrating nutrition interventions
alongside agricultural value chain interventions will contribute to a greater reduction in malnutrition among children under 3 years of age, compared to nutrition improvements anticipated from stand-­alone value chain activities.

The main objectives are to enable USAID missions to meet the performance monitoring requirements of Feed the Future and maximize the use and benefits of data collected; provide high-­quality empirical evidence to inform program design and investment decisions that will promote sustainable food security; ensure timely availability of high­quality data for use in monitoring performance and evaluating impacts of the Feed the Future initiative; and facilitate accountability and learning about which Feed the Future interventions work best, under what conditions, and at what cost.

We identified variables within the asset that present privacy risk (key variables) and applied the following techniques: a 3-anonymity technique on categorical key variables, such as geographic variables, household size, gender, and age. In order to reach the 3-anonymity threshold, we recoded some variables and suppressed values that increasedthe risk of re-identification. Doing so reduces the precision of the cells, while preserving statistical utility. 3-anonymity mitigates risk on key categorical variables in a combined way.

The survey collected information on about 4000 individuals in about 300 villages in 2 districts of Malawi. Highly detailed information was collected regarding children’s health and mothers’ health and their childbearing history, as well as detailed information about community health factors, and household expenditures.

resource.name: FTF "Don't Lose the Plot" Impact Assessment: Kenya Dataset
resource.description:
Dataset file can be found in the metadata below under "Attachments".

Feed the Future’s Africa Lead II project partnered with The Mediae Company, a Kenya-based media education company, to develop a pilot season of Africa’s first agriculture-focused reality TV program: Don’t Lose the Plot (DLTP). Targeting youth in Kenya and Tanzania, the show aired in Kenya and Tanzania between May and July 2017. The program’s objectives were to encourage youth to consider farming as a lucrative career choice, provide information on how to start agribusinesses, and share useful agronomic information. Africa Lead commissioned Kantar Public East Africa to evaluate the impact of DLTP on knowledge, attitudes, and behavior, or intention to change behavior, related to farming and agribusiness practices. 

This data asset includes quantitative data collected through a cross-sectional household survey in Kenya and Tanzania. Data collection took place between August and December 2017 and targeted both viewers and non-viewers of DLTP aged 18 to 35 years. A total sample of 3,737 target individuals were interviewed in Kenya, including 406 verified viewers. In Tanzania, 3,383 target individuals were interviewed, including 527 verified viewers.

resource.name: Ghana G-SAM Impact Evaluation Baseline Administrator Survey
resource.description: USAID’s Center of Excellence for Democracy, Human Rights and Governance contracted Social Impact, Inc. to conduct an impact evaluation of USAID’s Ghana Strengthening Accountability Mechanisms (G-SAM) program, which aimed to increase accountability of local District Assemblies in Ghana. This impact evaluation, a randomized-controlled trial, tested the effect of two distinct efforts to increase accountability and improve service delivery outcomes at the district level. One hundred fifty of Ghana’s districts were matched and randomized into one of three groups: a top-down treatment group that received performance audits conducted by the central government Ghana Audit Service (GAS); a bottom-up treatment group that received civil-society organization (CSO) led scorecard campaigns; and a control group that did not receive either intervention. Outcomes were measured across three surveys administered at baseline (2014) and endline (2017). This dataset specifically contains baseline data from a survey targeted at district administrations, who are responsible for overseeing the contracting and construction of development projects.

domain_metadata.value: Julia Kresky, Ben Morse, Erik Wibbels. 2023. Ghana G-SAM Impact Evaluation Baseline Administrator Survey. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/jhy5-ce9c.

As part of the de-identification process, we removed/recoded some geographic variables that may limit usability. In the household datasets, we removed village names and masked enumeration areas to prevent the risk of re-identification; this will prevent users from summarizing data at the village / EA levels, or tracking trends at these levels. Also to prevent the risk of re-identification, in the politician and administrator datasets, we removed district names and masked region names, which will make it impossible to associate responses with specific districts and regions.  Another limitation is that although the household survey was a panel survey, with the same households surveyed at baseline and endline, the household unique identifier is not available. As a result, households cannot be match across rounds and the data must be treated as a repeated cross section, rather than a panel survey.
Julia Kresky, Ben Morse, Erik Wibbels
Bureau for Development, Democracy, and Innovation

All datasets within this data asset have undergone an extensive de-identification process. The project team has reviewed each of the datasets individually for direct and indirect identifiers, including geographic variables. In consultation with Social Impact’s Institutional Review Board (IRB), we have removed all direct identifiers such as names, phone numbers, and physical addresses, as well as low-level geographic variables such as GPS coordinates, enumeration areas, and village names. We have also removed district names and encoded the region variable for the politician and administrator datasets due to the small number of politicians and administrators in each district and region. In addition, we recoded the age variable (transforming it from continuous to categorical) and recoded minority religious groups identified through the religion variable and minority tribal groups identified through the tribe variable as “Other.” We also reviewed all open-ended text variables and recoded any variables containing responses with potential PII as “missing.” This de-identified data asset has been approved for publication by the Social Impact IRB.  Please see the USAID Data Services DDL Variable Manipulation Overview, 
https://data.usaid.gov/api/views/xw2i-z7hr/files/de8f1fd7-1803-43bf-9a5a-de5f67a57ccb, noting the risk mitigation techniques implemented in some data assets on the DDL, as well as examples of the impact of these techniques on the data.

The data included in this data asset was collected as part of an impact evaluation of the Ghana Strengthening Accountability Mechanism’s (G-SAM) project, which aimed to improve accountability at the district level in Ghana. We believe this data would be a valuable resource for other researchers studying government accountability and could even be used to inform future good governance interventions across West Africa. The politician and administrator datasets capture information on the education and position of district-level administrators and politicians in Ghana, the perceived importance/ranking of factors that determine political success, factors that influence the types/locations of development projects, the process of identifying contractors for development projects and common issues in the construction or of these projects, perceived government corruption at the district level, the performance and provision of government services, and government accountability. The household datasets contain information on citizens’ views on the quality of services in their district, perceived factors that influence the type and location of development projects, perceived reasons for issues or other delays with projects in their district, the quality of governance and the political environment in their district, their participation in district politics and level of political sophistication, reported factors that influence their vote, perceived government accountability in their district, and levels of social cohesion in their community. Since this data asset contains three baseline datasets and three endline datasets each containing a wide range of variables, researchers who use this data asset will be able to understand changes in the above factors in Ghana over the 3-year period between 2014 and 2017.

resource.name: Baseline Study of Food for Peace Title II Development Food Assistance Program in Karamoja, Uganda--Asset Value and Consumption: Section 1
resource.description: This dataset contains the value of household assets and includes derived measures of daily per capita consumption.  This file has 206 columns and 4,723 rows.  It corresponds to Module H5 of the questionnaire.  In fiscal year 2012, USAID's Office of Food for Peace (FFP) awarded funding to private voluntary organizations (PVOs) to design and implement a multi-year Title II development food assistance program in Uganda.  The main purpose of the Title II program is to improve long-term food security of chronically food insecure population in the target regions.  FFP contracted a firm, ICF International to conduct a baseline study in targeted areas of the country prior to the start of the new program.  The purpose of the study was to assess the current status of key indicators, have a better understanding of prevailing conditions and perceptions of the population in the implementation areas, and serve as a point of comparison for future final evaluations.  Results would also be used to further refine program targeting and, where possible, to understand the relationship between variables to inform program design.  The study was conducted in 2013, while FFP expects to conduct final evaluations as close as possible to the end of the program five years later.  The data asset is comprised of six datasets: 1) a description of all members of the households surveyed, 2) data on maternal health and sanitation practices, 3) data about the children in the household, 4) data describing the agricultural practices of the household, 5) data describing the food consumption of the household (broken into 4 smaller spreadsheets), and 6) and a description of the weights that should be applied during the analysis of the other datasets. In the process of migrating data to the current DDL platform, datasets with a large number of variables required splitting into multiple spreadsheets.  They should be reassembled by the user to understand the data fully.

resource.name: Feed the Future Uganda Life of Activity Farmer Data: Year 2 Survey (October 2015 to March 2016)
resource.description: Life of activity farmer data (collected through Form 6 between October 2014 and September 2017) for the Feed the Future Uganda Commodity Production and Marketing Activity. This data was collected from farmers who have been reached through CPM-related interventions and broadly speaking, captures changes in adoption of CPM-promoted practices and the resulting impacts on production (i.e. improved quality and increased quantities produced). Moreover, Form 6 data supports reporting for nine Feed the Future indicators. In addition to the datasets, supporting documents include Form 6 survey tools used for each survey and calculation guides for computing the nine Feed the Future indicators that Form 6 measures.

domain_metadata.value: Chemonics International, Inc.. 2020. Feed the Future Uganda Life of Activity Farmer Data: Year 2 Survey (October 2015 to March 2016). Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/jqi5-qqfq.

The data was originally stripped of most PII at time of submission, including demographic
information of respondents (except the date of interview), GPS coordinates, and village information in some datasets. All of these PII have been removed as they provide no or limited usefulness to the data.

Agriculture is one of the most important components of the Ugandan economy, with 14 percent of gross domestic product, 85 percent of total export earning, and 73 percent of total employment. The Feed the Future intervention invested in increasing the production of maize, beans, and coffee through the appropriate use of high-quality agricultural inputs and decreasing the prevalence of counterfeit agricultural inputs, like mislabeled seeds or diluted fertilizers, in the market. It relied on an innovative market facilitation approach that empowers local actors such as the “Village Agent” to serve as role models in the agriculture industry and act as champions of best practices for the
way agricultural inputs are bought and sold.

resource.name: FTF Ghana 2015 Interim Population-Based Survey: Household Food Consumption in the Past 7 Days
resource.description: Feed the Future (FTF) initiative in Ghana is a collaborative effort that supports country-owned processes and plans for improving food security and nutrition, particularly in the northern part of the country. These datasets cover the interim survey that took place in 2015 and was designed as a follow-up to the baseline survey that happened from 2012 to 2013. The survey covered a range of indicators organized around four groups: (1) economic well-being; (2) women and children anthropometry; (3) hunger and diet diversity; and (4) women's empowerment. The survey design involved two stages in which enumeration areas were selected followed by households. Data was collected in a face-to-face fashion using well-designed questionnaires and other study materials.

Latitude and longitude structure of GPS have been removed. Data elements that carry no information value for research questions involving these data such as survey administration related data elements have been removed.
Data covers a wide range of indicators and variables that were included in the survey.

resource.description: This dataset contains variables from Module E, the Household Consumption Expenditures module used to calculate the poverty and expenditure indicators. The survey was designed to monitor program performance by periodic assessments of a number of standardized indicators.  A total of 1,021 households were interviewed, which provided data for the target sample size of 1,007 households and ensured the sample is representative of the seven districts covered in the interim assessment.  This dataset includes household-level derived variables (including the expenditure and poverty indicator variables), as well as variables from sub-Module E6: Housing Expenditures. The unique identifier in this household-level file is pbs_id.

resource.name: Genes Controlling Black Seed Coat and Pod Tip Color in Cowpea: Phenotype Data for the Sanzi by Vita 7 population
resource.description: Seed coat color is an important part of consumer preferences for cowpea (Vigna unguiculata [L.] Walp). Color has been studied in numerous crop species and has often been linked to loci controlling the anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway. This study makes use of available resources, including mapping populations, a reference genome, and a high-density single nucleotide polymorphism genotyping platform, to map the black seed coat and purple pod tip color traits, with the gene symbol Bl, in cowpea. Several gene models encoding MYB domain protein 113 were identified as candidate genes. MYB domain proteins have been shown in other species to control expression of genes encoding enzymes for the final steps in the anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway. PCR analysis indicated that a presence/absence variation of one or more MYB113 genes may control the presence or absence of black pigment. A PCR marker has been developed for the MYB113 gene Vigun05g039500, a candidate gene for black seed coat color in cowpea.

domain_metadata.value: University of California Riverside. 2023. Genes Controlling Black Seed Coat and Pod Tip Color in Cowpea: Phenotype Data for the Sanzi by Vita 7 population. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/jwzr-34nr.
Bureau for Resilience and Food Security

Advances in genomics over the past several years have enabled the elucidation the genetic basis of black seed coat and purple pod tip color, traits first described nearly one hundred years ago. This study maps black seed coat and purple pod tip color in several independently generated populations and provides candidate genes. Using high-throughput SNP genotyping and whole genome sequencing, previously impossible levels of mapping precision have been achieved. The presence of a deletion is supported by PCR evidence and sequence alignment from thirty-seven accessions. The identification of MYB transcription factors as candidate genes is supported by prior literature on homologous genes performing similar functions in other species, including Arabidopsis, grape, citrus, and soybean. The PCR-based markers developed here provide a useful tool for breeders engaged in marker-assisted selection for seed coat color in cowpea.

resource.description: Describes the test conducted and its results.  Multiple tests can be conducted for each individual sampled.

domain_metadata.value: PREDICT Consortium. 2022. PREDICT PCR Tests 3. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/jxk5-qdex.

All GPS locations are rounded to 2 decimal places (accuracy of about 1 km) to protect sensitive sampling sites related to wildlife. Direct and indirect identifiers have been removed from human data using HIPAA Privacy Rule guidance and human data are aggregated and summarized to further protect individuals sampled.

This data includes both a wide range of variables and rare and unique variables related to known and novel viruses, including where and in what species they were found. Data were collected in Africa and Asia in communities with high-risk wildlife contact and includes variables that can inform on risk associated with zoonotic pathogen transmission and potential targets for intervention to minimize risk of pathogen spillover.

resource.name: Section G Food Safety Measures
resource.description: The survey interviewed 254 retailer shops in 10 sub-cities of Addis Ababa. 30 supermarkets, 20 mini-markets, 100 regular shops, 80 dairy shops and 24 open market shops selling dairy products were interviewed. Details of the sampling strategy is found in the attachment. The survey collected information on the characteristics of the shop, details of dairy products sold, prices and quality. Policy makers, research, and other stakeholders can use this data to analyses dairy value chain in Ethiopia and dairy retailing practices in Ethiopia. This data set was collected through research of the project “Improving the evidence and policies for better performing livestock systems in Ethiopia” lead by the International Food Policy Research Institution as part of the Feed the Future Innovation Lab for Livestock Systems.

resource.name: Feed the Future Malawi Interim Survey in the Zone of Infuence, Children's File
resource.description: This dataset contains records describing for all children under 5 years of age sampled during the 2015 Feed the Future Malawi Interim Survey in the Zone of Influence.  The survey was designed to monitor program performance by periodic assessments of a number of standardized indicators.  A total of 1,021 households were interviewed, which provided data for the target sample size of 1,007 households and ensured the sample is representative of the seven districts covered in the interim assessment.  This dataset includes data from Module I for children’s anthropometry and infant and young child feeding practices. The anthropometry Z-scores were calculated in SAS during the data management process, using the World Health Organization (WHO) SAS “igrowup” package. The unique identifiers for this file are pbs_id + idcode.

resource.description: This dataset is the first of two interim surveys administered from October 2014 through April 2015 to enable the Feed the Future PRIME project in Ethiopia to monitor program performance by reviewing changes in a number of standardized indicators.  These indicators reflect data collected through population-based surveys (PBS) in the geographic areas targeted by Feed the Future interventions, known as the Feed the Future Zones of Influence (ZOI).  Each survey was administered to a sample of over 400 households in 17 kebeles (communities) once a month over a 6-month period creating for a total of six rounds of data for each survey.

resource.name: Crustaceans and Demersal, Large Pelagic and Small Pelagic Fish (Length Data)
resource.description:
Length data provides biological information and attributes of the catches of each sampled vessel that covers: organization/project; ID trip; surveyor; sampling; site sampling time; commodity; WPP; vessel name/owner; fishing gear; catcher; collector; fishing areas; total catch in volume (Kg); total catch in units (Ind); total sampling in volume (Kg); total sampling in units (Ind); sample name; total (Kg); units (Ind); length type; common name; species name; length (Cm).

The Length data is used best to assess the state of the fish stocks for fish species sampled using several modelling approaches such as the LBSPR (Length Based – Spawning Potential Ratio) that is, a relative rate of production in fish stock that have been exploited based on fish length. Other than that, this data also can provide 1) growth estimation parameter 2) Mortality 3) Fishing gear selectivity 4) recruitment pattern and 5) estimated fish mortality due to natural factors.

resource.name: Genes Controlling Black Seed Coat and Pod Tip Color in Cowpea: Output Data for the CB27 by IT82E-18 population
resource.description: Seed coat color is an important part of consumer preferences for cowpea (Vigna unguiculata [L.] Walp). Color has been studied in numerous crop species and has often been linked to loci controlling the anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway. This study makes use of available resources, including mapping populations, a reference genome, and a high-density single nucleotide polymorphism genotyping platform, to map the black seed coat and purple pod tip color traits, with the gene symbol Bl, in cowpea. Several gene models encoding MYB domain protein 113 were identified as candidate genes. MYB domain proteins have been shown in other species to control expression of genes encoding enzymes for the final steps in the anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway. PCR analysis indicated that a presence/absence variation of one or more MYB113 genes may control the presence or absence of black pigment. A PCR marker has been developed for the MYB113 gene Vigun05g039500, a candidate gene for black seed coat color in cowpea.

Bureau for Resilience and Food Security

Advances in genomics over the past several years have enabled the elucidation the genetic basis of black seed coat and purple pod tip color, traits first described nearly one hundred years ago. This study maps black seed coat and purple pod tip color in several independently generated populations and provides candidate genes. Using high-throughput SNP genotyping and whole genome sequencing, previously impossible levels of mapping precision have been achieved. The presence of a deletion is supported by PCR evidence and sequence alignment from thirty-seven accessions. The identification of MYB transcription factors as candidate genes is supported by prior literature on homologous genes performing similar functions in other species, including Arabidopsis, grape, citrus, and soybean. The PCR-based markers developed here provide a useful tool for breeders engaged in marker-assisted selection for seed coat color in cowpea.

As a part of the Citizens’ Voice Project (CVP), FAFEN trained domestic elections observers through a cascade training program implemented by six partner organizations in the formerly Federally Administrated Tribal Areas (FATA). The survey team conducted a telephonic survey of domestic observers to assess the understanding of their duties and the extent to which they were able to perform these duties on election day in the newly merged districts of the Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA).  Due to limited access to and large geographic spread of intervention districts, the survey team elected to conduct this survey telephonically. Telephone surveys have inherent limitations. First, the enumerator cannot gauge the body language of the respondent or easily develop a rapport. Second, the telephone survey may underrepresent the views of respondents in regions with poor telephone coverage. Third, the survey team anticipated a high non-response rate. To account for high non-response rates, the survey team increased the minimum required sample sizes for male and female trainers. The achieved sample sizes produced generalizable results within acceptable error limits (four percent absolute margin of error and 95 percent level of confidence for men; seven percent absolute margin of error and 95 percent level of confidence for women).

All unique individual identifiers, including names, addresses, and phone numbers of respondents, as well as names of data collection and processing teams, have been removed from the CVP survey dataset and omitted from the final report. A unique identification code was assigned to each survey respondent, reflecting respondents’ sex, training provider, and district. While these are important variables to explain variation in responses, together they do not provide sufficient information to identify individual respondents.

As a part of the Citizens’ Voice Project (CVP), FAFEN trained domestic elections observers through a cascade training program implemented by six partner organizations in the formerly Federally Administrated Tribal Areas (FATA). In September/October 2019, MSI conducted a telephonic survey of domestic observers of the former Federally Administered Tribal Areas (FATA), now referred to as the newly merged districts (NMDs) of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) province, to assess their understanding of their duties and the extent to which they were able to perform these duties on election day. The survey provides a quick snapshot of the effectiveness of capacity building efforts for elections observation in remote and difficult-to-access areas of the NMDs. The target population of the survey was 857 (773 male and 84 female) domestic observers trained by FAFEN through a cascade training. The minimum sample sizes required to produce representative results separately generalizable for male and female observers with four percent absolute margin of error and 95 percent level of confidence were 257 men and 68 women, respectively. In anticipation of high non-response rate in a telephonic survey format, the survey team increased its minimum required sample sizes for male and female observers to 589 and 84, respectively. From 773 male observers, the team selected 589 men using simple random sampling, and contacted all 84 women. The enumeration team successfully conducted 437 interviews, including 371 men and 66 women. The achieved sample sizes produced generalizable results within acceptable error limits (four percent absolute margin of error and 95 percent level of confidence for men; seven percent absolute margin of error and 95 percent level of confidence for women).The survey dataset provides respondent data relating to materials received during the training, satisfaction with and perceived utility of the training, knowledge of elections observation practices, and election day experiences (including access to polling stations, number of polling stations observed, permissions to partake in the vote counting process, violence or threats of violence received in the performance of one’s duties, and ability to upload observation data to the FAFEN data portal).In addition to the survey data, no other primary data was collected to inform the team’s analysis.

resource.name: Saving Lives at Birth DR Congo NeoBeat Study 2017: Liveborn App Dataset
resource.description:
The Newborn Heart Rate as a Catalyst for Improved Survival (NeoBeat Study) enrolled participants born between 1/1/17 and 06/22/20, with observational data collection beginning October 25, 2018. The primary purpose of this study was to evaluate the effect of resuscitation training and continuous electronic heart rate monitoring on total stillbirths. Three health facilities in Kinshasa, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, participated in the study. 

This dataset includes the observational data collected via an electronic tablet application, “Liveborn”, to document delivery room resuscitations.

domain_metadata.value: Jacquelyn Patterson, Daniel Ishoso, Daniel Ishoso, Joar Eilevstjønn, Melissa Bauserman, Ingunn Haug, Pooja Iyer, Beena D. Kamath-Rayne, Adrien Lokangaka, Casey Lowman, Eric Mafuta, Helge Myklebust, Tracy Nolen, Janna Patterson, Antoinette Tshefu, Carl Bose, Sara K. Berkelhamer

In 2015, approximately 2.6 million pregnancies reportedly ended in stillbirths; 98% occurred in low and lower-middle income countries (LMICs). Nearly one-half of stillbirths were classified as fresh stillbirths, indicating that the fetus died during the intrapartum period. Typically, the diagnosis of a stillbirth was made because the newborn did not breathe following birth. Yet many of these non-breathing newborns classified as stillborn have a heart rate (HR) and are actually live born. The effect of a low-cost monitor for measuring HR on newborn survival is unknown. Knowledge of HR during newborn resuscitation might also result in administration of appropriate interventions, and improvement in outcomes. Helping Babies Breathe (HBB), a resuscitation algorithm developed by the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), is widely accepted as the standard of care for newborn resuscitation in LMICs. In keeping with ILCOR recommendations that HR be measured during newborn resuscitation, HBB calls for heart rate assessment after 1 minute of positive-pressure ventilation with good chest movement (or sooner if there is a helper who can palpate/auscultate HR). However, given the frequent reality of a single provider attending deliveries in LMICs, as well as the currently available methods for assessing HR (i.e. palpation or auscultation), assessment of HR is challenging to perform without delaying or stopping the provision of other life-saving interventions such as bag and mask ventilation.  Furthermore, the most accurate method of HR assessment at birth is an electrocardiogram, which is not widely available in LMICs. NeoBeat is a low-cost alternative to continuously monitor HR that can guide resuscitation in these settings.

The data and metadata that comprise this open access, peer-reviewed technical publication provide insight into the composition and architecture of the genome of cowpea via a high-quality, annotated genome sequence. The annotations include genes, repetitive sequences and positions of nearly one million genetic variants that exist within cultivated cowpeas. Relationships of the cowpea genome to common bean is highlighted, and each cowpea chromosome is mathematically described as recombination rate as a function of nucleotide position. This information provides a framework upon which to hang all past and future information about genetic variation within the species, as well as suites of genetic markers for any trait that has been or will be genetically mapped. Such information is useful for marker-assisted breeding, and to spawn basic research on mechanisms underlying the range of traits of cowpea.

resource.name: Genes Controlling Black Seed Coat and Pod Tip Color in Cowpea: Primer information used for determining the size of the deletion and as the PCR marker
resource.description: Seed coat color is an important part of consumer preferences for cowpea (Vigna unguiculata [L.] Walp). Color has been studied in numerous crop species and has often been linked to loci controlling the anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway. This study makes use of available resources, including mapping populations, a reference genome, and a high-density single nucleotide polymorphism genotyping platform, to map the black seed coat and purple pod tip color traits, with the gene symbol Bl, in cowpea. Several gene models encoding MYB domain protein 113 were identified as candidate genes. MYB domain proteins have been shown in other species to control expression of genes encoding enzymes for the final steps in the anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway. PCR analysis indicated that a presence/absence variation of one or more MYB113 genes may control the presence or absence of black pigment. A PCR marker has been developed for the MYB113 gene Vigun05g039500, a candidate gene for black seed coat color in cowpea.

domain_metadata.value: University of California Riverside. 2023. Genes Controlling Black Seed Coat and Pod Tip Color in Cowpea: Primer information used for determining the size of the deletion and as the PCR marker. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/khcc-vzez.
Bureau for Resilience and Food Security

Advances in genomics over the past several years have enabled the elucidation the genetic basis of black seed coat and purple pod tip color, traits first described nearly one hundred years ago. This study maps black seed coat and purple pod tip color in several independently generated populations and provides candidate genes. Using high-throughput SNP genotyping and whole genome sequencing, previously impossible levels of mapping precision have been achieved. The presence of a deletion is supported by PCR evidence and sequence alignment from thirty-seven accessions. The identification of MYB transcription factors as candidate genes is supported by prior literature on homologous genes performing similar functions in other species, including Arabidopsis, grape, citrus, and soybean. The PCR-based markers developed here provide a useful tool for breeders engaged in marker-assisted selection for seed coat color in cowpea.

resource.name: Feed the Future Senegal: Yaajeende Production Data
resource.description:
The purpose of this study is to evaluate the impact that the Feed the Future Nutrition-led Agriculture Project for Food Security in Senegal (known as "Yaajeende") has had on reducing malnutrition and poverty in its intervention area.

This report details the findings, conclusions and recommendations of a mixed-methods quasi-experimental final impact evaluation (FIE) of the United States Agency for International Development’s (USAID) $50 million, seven-year Feed the Future Nutrition-Led Agriculture Project for Food Security in Senegal, known as “Yaajeende.” The National Cooperative Business Association’s Cooperative League of the USA (NCBA CLUSA) implemented the project. To combat poverty and child malnutrition, Yaajeende sought to accelerate the participation of the very poor in rural economic growth and improve the four dimensions of food security: availability, access, utilization and stability. Yaajeende worked in 790 villages across 49 municipalities (“communes” in French) and nine departments in the Matam, Tambacounda, Kédougou and Kolda regions. The project’s implementation period was November 1, 2010, to September 30, 2017.

The FIE aims to provide USAID with an evidence base on the impacts of the nutrition-led agriculture (NLA) approach that the project utilized on its key objectives, including reduced poverty and malnutrition. The findings are expected to provide accountability and learning value to USAID, including both the Senegal Mission and USAID/Feed the Future. Additional stakeholders include the Government of Senegal, implementing partners and other agencies, donors and practitioners active in nutrition, health, agriculture and integrated sectors.

The Kenya Agricultural Value Chain Enterprises (KAVES) activity works with smallholder farmers, businesses, and national and county government partners to address constraints up and down the value chain (such as agro-processors, input suppliers, transporters, exporters, retailers, financiers) and develop fully-functioning, competitive value chains. resource.name: USAID Workforce Demographic Data 2021
resource.description:
This data asset was created in response to House Report 117-401, which stated, "The Committee directs the USAID Administrator, in consultation with the Director of 
the Office of Personnel Management and the Director of the Office of Management and Budget, to submit a report to the appropriate congressional committees, not later than 180 days after enactment of this Act, on USAID's workforce data that 
includes disaggregated demographic data and other information regarding the diversity of the workforce of USAID. Such report shall include the following data to the maximum extent practicable and permissible by law: 1) demographic data of 
USAID workforce disaggregated by grade or grade-equivalent; 2) assessment of agency compliance with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission Management Directive 715; and 3) data on the overall number of individuals who are part of the workforce, including all U.S. Direct Hires, personnel under personal services contracts, and Locally Employed staff at USAID. The report shall also be published on a publicly available website of USAID in a searchable database format."  This data asset fulfills the final part of this requirement, to publish the data in a searchable database format.

The data are compiled from USAID's 2021 MD-715 report, available at https://www.usaid.gov/who-we-are/organization/independent-offices/office-civil-rights/md-715-reports.  The original data source is the system National Finance Center Insight owned by the Treasury Department.  This dataset reports demographic data for the USAID workforce for fiscal year 2021.

To support USAID/Kenya’s mission to empower youth as envisioned in Kenya’s 2010 constitution, YYC developed peaceful leaders among 18- to 35-year-olds while improving the youths’ socioeconomic status. resource.name: Survey data for weed seedbank across farms with varying tillage practices in Eastern India
resource.description: This project compiled germinable seedbank counts from 84 farmers’ fields in Bihar and Eastern Uttar Pradesh, India. Soil samples were submitted for soil texture and chemical analyses. Seedbank soil samples were collected from pairs of neighboring fields with similar soils and microclimates but differing in historic tillage (conventional tillage [CT] versus zero tillage [ZT]) and crop rotation practices (rice­-wheat versus rice­maize/potato-­rice­-wheat).
resource.attribution: US Borlaug Fellows in Global Food Security

domain_metadata.value: Carolyn Lowry. 2020. Survey data for weed seedbank across farms with varying tillage practices in Eastern India. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/m7vb-rcbw.
Time required for manuscript preparation after data submission.

Soil samples for weed seedbank analysis were collected from pairs of neighboring fields with similar soils and microclimates but differing in tillage and crop rotation practices, across three regions in Bihar and Eastern Uttar Pradesh: Samastipur-Vaishali-Muzaffarpur (SVM), Ara-Buxar (AB) and Maharajgunj-Kushinagar (MK). In total we collected soil from 84 farmer fields. Soil samples were collected to a depth of 15 cm from each field following rice harvest but before wheat planting. Soil cores from each fieldwere composited and air dried until the germination assay. We utilized 2 subsamples of 500 ml of soil each from each farm for seedbank analysis. Soils were brought to a common greenhouse, spread in a thin layer in flats, and evaluated for germinable seedbank through exhaustive germination; soil subsamples were analysed for soil texture, and soil chemical characteristics including pH, electrical conductivity (EC), organic carbon (OC), P, K, Mg and Ca.

resource.name: Feed the Future Tanzania Mboga na Matunda Private Sector Survey 2019 - Module H Service Sales
resource.description: This data asset contains data from the beneficiary based fiscal year 2019 annual results survey of private sector firms assisted by the Feed the Future Tanzania - Mboga na Matunda Project. The project works to improve the livelihoods of horticultural farmers in the regions of Iringa, Morogoro, Songwe, Mbeya, and Zanzibar, and strengthen the market system throughout the ZOI. The survey sample was developed using one level of stratification, firm type. Firms were selected from five different categories: Processor, Buyer, Local input supplier, Regional input supplier, Finance provider, and Other service provider. In total, 321 firms were surveyed. The data is split into modules. Module A captures basic identifying data on the firm. Module B captures information on the proprietors. Modules C, D, E, F, G and H capture data on sales of products and services. Module I captures information on business practices. Module J captures information on production costs. Module K captures information on access to finance.

All survey specific data elements should be removed as they are only useful in managing the implementation of the survey: date of interview, ability to be interviewed alone, outcome of the interview.

A range of household level data elements were reported in all other datasets and should be removed from all datasets except household’s. Examples include dwelling characteristics (roof, floor, walls) and hunger scale questions.

We will use the following steps to anonymize the datasets:
1.	Use k-anonymity to mitigate the following variables: sex, dwelling characteristics, relationship to household head, type of toilets, education level, literacy level (read and write), district, urbanization. To achieve a threshold of k=3, we will recode some of these variables including dwelling characteristics, type of toilets, relationship to household head, education level, and literacy level  
2.	Aggregate age variable into 5 ages bands. 
3.	Apply a micro aggregation to children and women weights and heights. Micro Aggregation replaces each single value with local means calculated on batches of 3 records each. 
4.	Top code the age and estimated price of house. Any reported house age value above 100 years was recoded as 100; any estimated price at 5 000 000 or above was replaced with the mean price of houses costing 5 000 000 or more. 
5.	      5. Capping household size to 13. To achieve this, we will randomly select out of the datasets individual members from these large households who do not participate anywhere else in the survey other than their membership to household. Initially, the largest household had 21 members; after this process, this household would have 13 members. The median household in Kenya is about 4.4. In this data, the median remains at 5.0 before and after households disclosure risk mitigation.

resource.name: Ethiopia Land Governance Activity Baseline Survey 2021: Dataset
resource.description: This dataset, containing 171 rows and 150 columns, presents the results of the quantitative baseline study conducted in the pilot urban and peri-urban areas of Dukem Town, from January 20, 2021 to February 20, 2021, to establish baseline data for comparison to support the program impact measurement as part of future project evaluation and to guide a realistic and feasible target setting for the selected performance indicators. A household survey was administered to a representative sample of 171 households (out of the 1,500 targeted households) in Dukem town to collect quantitative data with a questionnaire length of an average of 50 minutes. All personally identifiable information (e.g., GIS data) was removed from the dataset to protect the personal information of survey respondents. The Feed the Future Ethiopia Land Governance Activity (LGA) is a five-year project funded by USAID, following three successfully implemented land governance projects it supported during 2005 – 2018, i.e. (i) Ethiopia Land Tenure Administration Project (ELTAP) 2005- 2008; Ethiopia Land Administration Project (ELAP) 2008-2013, and Land Administration to Nurture Development (LAND) 2013-2018.

resource.name: Baseline Study of Food for Peace Title II Development Food Assistance Program in Karamoja, Uganda--Child Health
resource.description: This dataset describes the children and their health interviewed as part of Baseline Study of Food for Peace Title II Development Food Assistance Program in Karamoja, Uganda.  This dataset contains data from Module D of the questionnaire and has 201 columns and 6,001 rows.  In fiscal year 2012, USAID's Office of Food for Peace (FFP) awarded funding to private voluntary organizations (PVOs) to design and implement a multi-year Title II development food assistance program in Uganda.  The main purpose of the Title II program is to improve long-term food security of chronically food insecure population in the target regions.  FFP contracted a firm, ICF International to conduct a baseline study in targeted areas of the country prior to the start of the new program.  The purpose of the study was to assess the current status of key indicators, have a better understanding of prevailing conditions and perceptions of the population in the implementation areas, and serve as a point of comparison for future final evaluations.  Results would also be used to further refine program targeting and, where possible, to understand the relationship between variables to inform program design.  The study was conducted in 2013, while FFP expects to conduct final evaluations as close as possible to the end of the program five years later.  The data asset is comprised of six datasets: 1) a description of all members of the households surveyed, 2) data on maternal health and sanitation practices, 3) data about the children in the household, 4) data describing the agricultural practices of the household, 5) data describing the food consumption of the household (broken into 4 smaller spreadsheets), and 6) and a description of the weights that should be applied during the analysis of the other datasets.

resource.name: Genes Controlling Black Seed Coat and Pod Tip Color in Cowpea: Allele effects of significant SNPs showing the highest association with black seed coat and purple pod tip color in the minicore population
resource.description: Seed coat color is an important part of consumer preferences for cowpea (Vigna unguiculata [L.] Walp). Color has been studied in numerous crop species and has often been linked to loci controlling the anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway. This study makes use of available resources, including mapping populations, a reference genome, and a high-density single nucleotide polymorphism genotyping platform, to map the black seed coat and purple pod tip color traits, with the gene symbol Bl, in cowpea. Several gene models encoding MYB domain protein 113 were identified as candidate genes. MYB domain proteins have been shown in other species to control expression of genes encoding enzymes for the final steps in the anthocyanin biosynthesis pathway. PCR analysis indicated that a presence/absence variation of one or more MYB113 genes may control the presence or absence of black pigment. A PCR marker has been developed for the MYB113 gene Vigun05g039500, a candidate gene for black seed coat color in cowpea.

domain_metadata.value: University of California Riverside. 2023. Genes Controlling Black Seed Coat and Pod Tip Color in Cowpea: Allele effects of significant SNPs showing the highest association with black seed coat and purple pod tip color in the minicore population. Dataset. USAID Development Data Library. https://data.usaid.gov/d/mr86-xkg5.
Bureau for Resilience and Food Security

Advances in genomics over the past several years have enabled the elucidation the genetic basis of black seed coat and purple pod tip color, traits first described nearly one hundred years ago. This study maps black seed coat and purple pod tip color in several independently generated populations and provides candidate genes. Using high-throughput SNP genotyping and whole genome sequencing, previously impossible levels of mapping precision have been achieved. The presence of a deletion is supported by PCR evidence and sequence alignment from thirty-seven accessions. The identification of MYB transcription factors as candidate genes is supported by prior literature on homologous genes performing similar functions in other species, including Arabidopsis, grape, citrus, and soybean. The PCR-based markers developed here provide a useful tool for breeders engaged in marker-assisted selection for seed coat color in cowpea.

resource.description:
The Kenya Agricultural Value Chain Enterprises (KAVES) activity works with smallholder farmers, businesses, and national and county government partners to address constraints up and down the value chain (such as agro-processors, input suppliers, transporters, exporters, retailers, financiers) and develop fully-functioning, competitive value chains. KAVES aims to increase the productivity and incomes of smallholder farmers, and other actors along the value chain, who are working in the dairy, maize (and other staples), and horticulture sectors.
